answer.exemplar: A null fringe shift means that the apparatus detected no difference in the round-trip travel time of the light beams along perpendicular arms, so there is no detectable wind of space carrying the light. questions.learningObjective: Explain why no massive object can reach the speed of light.
questions.stem: A student asks why a particle that is accelerated harder and harder never passes the speed of light. Explain the role of the Lorentz factor in the answer.

answer.exemplar: The energy of a particle of rest mass m is gamma times m c squared, and gamma is 1 over the square root of one minus beta squared. questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a null fringe shift rules out
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether an observed fringe shift is small enough to be null.
questions.stem: An interferometer report quotes an expected fringe shift of 0.42 and an observed shift of 0.14 for the same apparatus. By what factor is the observed shift smaller than the expected one?
questions.explanation: The expected shift divided by the observed one is 0.42/0.14 = 3, so the leftover is a third of the signal and does not count as null. A genuine drift would have produced the full expected size.
questions.hint: Divide the expected shift by the observed shift.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The postulate that removes a preferred frame
questions.learningObjective: Derive the speed of light and connect it to the frame-independent postulate.
questions.stem: A lecture slide asks for the speed of light implied by a measured frequency of 4.00e14 hertz and a measured wavelength of 750 nanometres, and for the principle that keeps the value the same in every frame.

options.text: 3.00e8 metres per second, because the wavelength and frequency always cancel the frame motion.
options.misconception: invents a cancellation in product instead of citing

options.text: 3.00e8 metres per second, because every inertial observer measures the same light speed.
1.33e8 metres per second, because the wavelength was quoted in nanometres directly.
options.misconception: uses the wavelength number without converting units

options.text: 3.00e8 metres per second, because the speed of light depends on the source's motion.
options.misconception: gives right number but denies invariance of speed

questions.explanation: Wavelength times frequency gives 750e-9 x 4.00e14 = 3.00e8 metres per second, and every inertial frame obtains that same value. A moving source changes the frequency, not the speed.
questions.hint: Multiply wavelength by frequency, then cite the postulate.
